item.title: Autism Underrepresented Among Women and Minority Identities
item.description:
Autism

Autism Underrepresented Among Women and Minority Identities

Why we need more neuro-affirming practices in schools, healthcare, and workplaces.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • There is a better understanding of the subtle and less obvious presentations of autism.
  • Autism has been identified more in girls and women in recent years.
  • Autism has been identified more often in children from underrepresented backgrounds in recent years.

Autism is characterized by differences in social interactions, nonverbal communication, and relationship style, as well as at least two of the following traits: repetitive movements, strong interests, sensory sensitivities, and/or differences in cognitive flexibility. Autism is a developmental disorder, and there must be evidence of some autistic traits from early childhood.

The subtle and less obvious presentations of autism are better understood. For example, some autistic people can mask or camouflage their traits more than others in daily life. Many people with autism engage in eye contact when interacting with others and can be exceptionally empathic, two behaviors that used to be thought to contraindicate autism.

The advocacy and pioneering work of many people with different presentations of autistic traits has gained the attention of practitioners and scientists. The field has a better understanding of the multitude of ways in which autism and autistic traits manifest. Data suggest these efforts are having an impact.

The identification of autism is increasing dramatically

For example, from 2011 to 2022, autism diagnoses increased by 175%, up to 6.3 per 1,000 persons (Grosvenor et al., 2024).

Increases were greater for female children (305%) than male children (185%) and greater in female adults (315%) than male adults (215%).

Autism rates increased more in adulthood (ages 25-34, 452%; ages 35-44, 338%)—and at the youngest ages (ages 0-4, 352% increase)—more than in children (ages 5-8, 207%; ages 9-12, 143%).

Autism was identified more in Black, Asian, American Indian or Alaska Native, and Hispanic children than in White children, but racial and ethnic disparities in Autism persisted in adult groups. For example, an autism diagnosis was more common in Whites than in Hispanic and Black adults.

The recognition of autism is predicted to grow

These data are eye-opening. Widespread implementation of neuro-affirmative care and practices is needed. Schools, health care offices, and workplaces can create environments where all children and adults feel safe and thrive.

Neuro-affirming practices involve a shift in framework and priorities to recognize behavior and communication, and to support self-regulation, autonomy, self-advocacy, and independence. Practical advice to achieve these goals is available for schools (e.g., Kircher-Morris and Morin, 2025), workplaces (Fitzell, 2025), and healthcare settings (Miral, 2025).

Small changes can make a big difference. Using neurodiversity-affirming language can be a powerful intervention and is characterized by neutrality, emphasizing strengths and abilities, and using less medicalized language (e.g., she had autistic traits versus autistic symptoms) (Kircher-Morris and Morin, 2025).

Universal design is a method for creating environments (e.g., buildings, schools) and products (e.g., software) that are accessible to as many people as possible (Kircher-Morris and Morin, 2025). Universal design removes barriers. The principle of universal design can help maximize the comfort and success of everyone and include equitable access, flexibility, simplicity, intuition, effective communication of information, tolerance for mistakes, low physical effort, and appropriate size and space.

Open-mindedness to functioning differently and better—in all aspects of society—is exciting and deserves attention. Greater accessibility of opportunity benefits everyone.

item.title: The Words 'I Don't Know' May Limit Us
item.description:
Therapy

The Words 'I Don't Know' May Limit Us

We have the urge to answer too quickly, but we can let curiosity do its work.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Speech-act theory shows that words can perform actions rather than merely communicate information.
  • “I don’t know” can end self-reflection before possible answers have time to emerge.
  • “If I had to guess” keeps curiosity alive without requiring immediate certainty.

Speech-Act Theory

J. L. Austin was an English philosopher best known for developing speech-act theory. Austin observed that words do not merely describe; at times they also perform an action.

When someone says, “I forgive you,” they are not solely communicating information about forgiveness. They are also doing something. The relationship between the two of you is different after those words have been spoken. Likewise, phrases such as “I promise,” “I apologize,” and “I accept” alter the social world between two or more individuals simply by the act of being said.

Most people move through life unaware of this power. They imagine words as sounds that carry thoughts from one person to another. But words can direct attention, assign meaning, establish identities, and most importantly for this post: determine which questions can be explored.

The Power of Words

Therapy often involves discovering how words spoken long ago continue to live inside us. Perhaps a childhood nickname such as “drama queen” or “the shy one” gradually shaped a person’s self-concept. What began as a teasing observation became a family role. Repeated expressions can have similar effects. “Boys don’t cry.” “Nothing tastes as good as skinny feels.” “We don’t talk about family business.” These phrases may be spoken casually yet have profound influence on an individual’s relationship with emotion, food, or vulnerability. It is no surprise that research generally associates warm, open parent-child communication with better outcomes, while hostile, negative, and inconsistent communication is associated with poorer well-being (Grey and colleagues, 2022).

Yet some of the most influential words in our lives are no longer being spoken by our parents. They are the words we have learned to repeat to ourselves.

A Spell of Denial

Over my years as a therapist, I have become particularly interested in three words that can exert an unnoticed and often oversized effect on therapy: “I don’t know.”

A therapist might ask:

“Where do you think you learned that?”
“When was the first time you remember comparing yourself to another person?”
“What do you imagine would happen if you disappointed your mother?”

Sometimes “I don’t know” is an answer. Sometimes it’s a spell we cast on ourselves to keep us from exploring deeper.
Source: AI Generated

Often, “I don’t know” escapes the mouth of a client before they have spent even five seconds considering the question.

Self-exploration is difficult work. If we knew all of the answers to how we arrived at the person who we are today, we may not need psychotherapy. But “I don’t know” can also do more than describe uncertainty. It can be an unconscious defense mechanism to end the search for an answer before it even begins.

While outwardly the phrase may express “I do not have an answer,” the words may be performing an action: “I will not consider this question.” Curiosity withdraws. Possibilities that might have emerged if we're willing to experience some silent consideration are dismissed before they can take form.

We stop looking.

It is almost as though we cast a small spell of denial over ourselves. The spell does not erase knowledge. It protects us from approaching whatever the search might uncover.

The Yes, And of Therapy

There is a useful parallel in improv comedy. The foundational principle of improv is “yes, and.” When one performer introduces an idea, the other accepts the premise and contributes something to it. If the second performer immediately denies the invitation, the scene collapses. Creative movement requires temporarily allowing an uncertain possibility to exist.

Self-reflection requires something similar. We do not need to know that our first answer is correct. We only need to let an answer enter the room.

Instead of I don’t know:

“The first thing that comes to mind is…”
“If I had to guess…”
“Part of me wonders whether…”
“I notice that I don’t want to answer that.”
“Nothing is coming up yet. Can I sit with it for a moment?”

Let a question stay open a little longer to give yourself time to consider possible answers.
Source: AI Generated

These responses do not pretend to possess certainty about your story, but they keep the process of self-examination moving. The first thought does not need to be a final pronouncement of truth, but it most certainly can be material worth examining.

Therapy does not require you to know the answer. It asks for something both smaller and more difficult: that you remain curious long enough for an answer to become possible.

“I don’t know” may be what is stopping you from the work really beginning.

item.title: Misophonia, Speeding Slowly Toward the Gap
item.description:
Misophonia

Misophonia, Speeding Slowly Toward the Gap

How dynamics outside of the condition help to define misophonia.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • Gaps in our knowledge about misophonia exceed what we know.
  • The generative power of individual disciplines helps create scientific knowledge.
  • Binary thinking can get in the way of understanding the dynamics of knowledge production.
Source: Altotemi/Creative Commons

Shape clay into a vessel;

It is the space within that makes it useful.

Cut doors and windows for a room;

It is the holes which make it useful.

Verse 11, Tao Te Ching

When our family was new to misophonia in 2019, I felt surrounded by a whole lot of nothing. Everywhere we turned for research-based help and information, we came up empty-handed. No definition, no treatment, no professional help. Lack defined our experience. Each gap felt cruel.

What I couldn’t yet see is how productive those empty spaces were. The Tao Te Ching illuminates the flexible purposes emptiness can serve. Holes in a wall are not void, but complexly utilitarian. Human beings are impelled toward meaning. How do we define that empty space: vessel, door, or window? We don’t simply experience our circumstances. We give meaning and purpose to the forces shaping our lives.

The search for meaning takes on urgency when suffering is involved. Although most of misophonia’s terrain remains uncharted (empty), emerging research and anecdotal evidence expose legions of pain: about 5% of people experience clinically significant misophonia symptoms (Dixon et al., 2024). Consider the spheres of relationships that surround each of these people, and suffering ripples through millions more.

As a mother, sister-in-law, and daughter-in-law caught up in misophonia’s thrall, I have witnessed and experienced the condition’s devastation across generations. Misophonia’s terrible threats to intimacy separated me from my child. Although we lived in the same house, we painfully avoided each other’s presence for years. We did not talk or touch. Our experience is not uncommon. In families with misophonia, parents can lose straightforward access to children; siblings retreat and grow apart; life can be reduced to a lonely ordeal for all. No wonder the quest to better understand this condition occupies so many of us.

From professional scientist to conventionally credentialed therapist, to alternative practitioner (for example, homeopath, hypnotist), to parents like me, different types of people invested in misophonia have differing ideas ready to fill many voids. This vast network is producing a robust and decidedly confusing “misophonia marketplace” of ideas and therapies.

Although theories outside of professional science influence misophonia in varied and often invisible ways, professional science dominates this field of knowledge—which does not guarantee accuracy or even smooth sailing. Professional science is an industry of research within networks of government, healthcare, and university bureaucracies. This slow-moving sphere of knowledge production is not a space of unified or even compatible thinking.

Science is a tremendously heterogeneous network: scores of individual disciplines are grouped into broad categories of natural, social, and applied sciences. Most misophonia research comes from audiology, neuroscience, and psychology, nestling the field between natural and social sciences. After elbowing out so much competition, which or what combination of these three disciplines might ultimately define the field?

Staying with the concept of “emptiness” helps answer this question.

Imagine a sandy shoreline. A huge hole has been abandoned by the child who dug it. Waves lap a few feet away. The sun beats down and the wind flutters. The hole will fill with water, sand, or some seepy combination. How this happens and which dominates (sand or water) is determined by forces outside and independent of the hole. Gravity, tide, sand and other environmental elements determine what fills the hole—and let’s not forget rain, or the whims of beachgoers and their dogs, at a minimum. Nothing bubbles up from within. Processes outside of the hole control its future.

Knowledge production follows a similar pattern. Forces outside of misophonia determine what fills the gap. This counters our ideal of scientific knowledge as an enterprise of objectivity that excavates essential or organic attributes. For misophonia, tide and the random kick aren’t at play, but conditions equally distant from (and even disinterested in) misophonia are, including but not limited to, money, employment, and the self-sustaining, generative power of individual disciplines and institutions.

Money is the most obvious example of this dynamic. Before the 2019 creation of the Misophonia Research Fund (MRF), money for misophonia research was a dribble. Fewer than 60 published papers span the condition’s first 18 years of scientific existence.

Founded by the parents of a child with misophonia, MRF’s influx of capital proved to be a high-octane jumpstart: search PubMed today and you'll find over 400 studies and commentaries on misophonia, an increase of some 560%. An editorial introducing a 2023 misophonia-focused edition of Frontiers in Neuroscience credits the fund for the significant uptick in “the pace and quality of scientific research” (Rosenthal et al., 2023).

Money fills the gap.

MRF greased wheels that allowed studies in audiology, neuroscience, and psychology to roll in. Among these, psychology dominates. Think Swiss cheese, with psychology filling most gaps. Does that mean psychology is the condition’s appropriate conceptual home? Not necessarily.

Psychology had a big head start, and the wind remains at its back. The discipline stands out for its cultural clout and already-existing dominance in our daily lives. Psychology has spawned the concepts we use to explain relating—and we relate to pretty much everything, from objects and creatures in the world, to other people, to aspects of our own selves. A quick tour of the many topics covered on this website, Psychology Today, reveals the discipline's expansive terrain.

Among the phalanx of scholars studying knowledge production, sociologist Nikolas Rose is notable for his assertion that psychology and related “psy” disciplines like psychiatry, play an outsize role in shaping our understanding of human interiority. Universal human processes from thinking to emoting to perceiving (seeing, hearing, feeling, etc.), are all bound up in the discipline's domain. Rose and other critics question the veracity of psychology's claims on human interiority.

Do these dynamics warrant a wholesale rejection of psychology as a legitimate misophonia authority? Not at all. The good/bad swivel of binary thinking does not serve us here.

For example, not only does the majority of misophonia research come from psychology, the influential Duke Center for Misophonia and Emotion (CMER), is primarily staffed and steered by psychologists/psychiatrists and psychology students. The advances in understanding misophonia's embodied processes and tiptoe steps into clinical care brought to us by CMER and other misophonia research hubs around the world are profoundly positive, hopeful developments.

Still, those of us invested in misophonia’s future must be aware of the existing forces (akin to rain or sand) driving misophonia research. We continue to circle those blank spaces in misophonia. Window, vessel, door: who gets to inscribe misophonia's meaning?

These uncertain processes are not easy for families like mine, where ending suffering is not an abstraction, but a series of daily decisions through webs of sight and sound. We don't just experience these circumstances. We yearn for meaning and a purposeful path through the void—help that is still taking its shape.

As our families receive an influx of psychological theories about misophonia, it is important to keep our eyes on the dynamics driving these theories into the void and our attention. Misophonia's meaning remains in the making. Perhaps psychology's current dominance in the field tells us as much about knowledge production as it does about misophonia.

item.title: Why Calling Your Child Picky May Matter More Than You Think
item.description:
Parenting

Why Calling Your Child Picky May Matter More Than You Think

How labels shape self-identity.

Posted July 22, 2026

"We have two kids. One eats everything, and the other is our picky eater."

I've heard some version of this countless times from parents. Most say it without hesitation, as if they're simply describing reality. But what if that label is doing more than describing a child's eating? What if it's quietly shaping how everyone, including the child, thinks about their eating habits?

Psychologists have long recognized that children build their sense of self through their interactions with the people and world around them. The messages that they hear from their parents, teachers, and other caregivers become part of the story that they tell themselves.

Labels and Identity Formation

"I'm just a picky eater."

Psychologists refer to this process as identity formation. Children actively construct beliefs about themselves based on their experiences and the feedback that they receive from others. Those beliefs, in turn, influence future behavior. When a child comes to see themselves as someone who doesn't eat unfamiliar foods, avoiding those foods begins to feel consistent with who they are.

Expectations can reinforce this process. Over time, the child receives repeated messages about who they are: I don't like vegetables. I'm not adventurous with food. I'm a picky eater. As these beliefs become a part of their identity, trying something new may feel less like tasting a different food and more like acting against their sense of self. In this way, selective eating can become maintained not only by taste preferences but also by identity and expectation.

"Picky Eating" in Normal Development

Many children are naturally cautious eaters. Food neophobia, or a reluctance to try unfamiliar foods, is a normal stage of development that typically peaks between the ages of two and seven. This correlates with their budding independence and their desire to test out control of their environment. It was also likely beneficial from an evolutionary perspective, because wariness around unfamiliar foods likely discouraged young children from eating something harmful.

While food neophobia is a normal and often temporary stage of development, the way adults respond to these behaviors can influence whether children gradually expand their food preferences or become more restricted over time. In many cases, well-intentioned reactions can unintentionally reinforce selective eating habits.

Consider what happens when a child refuses new foods or shows strong preferences for certain foods or food groups. Their parent says, "She's our picky eater." Grandparents hear the label and may stop serving vegetables when she visits, planning instead for all her favorites. Parents may shy away from new recipes because “there’s no way she’ll eat it.” Family may just order her chicken fingers whenever they go to a restaurant because "that's all she'll eat." The label "picky" is now shaping her opportunities and experiences for growth and learning as well. This quickly turns her limited palate into a self-fulfilling prophecy, limiting opportunities for the true thing that helps children learn to eat new foods: exposure.

Changing the Narrative

Fortunately, identities are not fixed, and children’s food preferences are far more flexible than many parents assume. Just as children can come to see themselves as "picky eaters," they can also begin to view themselves as curious, capable, and willing to try new things. Small, positive experiences with food, especially when adults avoid labels and emphasize exploration rather than pressure, can gradually reshape those beliefs. Rather than reinforcing the identity of a picky eater, caregivers can foster an identity of a child who is still learning, growing, and becoming more confident with new foods.

Most food preferences are learned through experience and are not innately formed. Research shows that repeated, pressure-free exposure increases acceptance of unfamiliar foods. Seeing a food on the table, helping prepare it, smelling it, touching it, and eventually tasting it all contribute to learning. This process often does require many more exposures than parents expect, however, often as high as 15 to 20 times per food.

Supporting a Growth Mindset

Eating should be viewed less as a personality trait and more as a developmental skill. That shift changes the narrative around children’s eating. Rather than describing a child as a picky eater, parents could consider saying “he’s still learning to like new foods,” or “he’s not comfortable with that food yet.” These aren't empty reassurances, but instead describe eating as something that can change with experience rather than something that’s fixed about a child's character.

Parents can also focus on positive behaviors instead of generalized labels. Rather than praising a child for being "a good eater" or criticizing them for being "picky," they can acknowledge acts of exploration: noticing a new food, helping cook it, smelling it, touching it, or taking a small taste. These behaviors reflect growing confidence, even if they don't immediately result in an empty plate. By celebrating curiosity instead of the number of bites consumed, parents encourage children to see themselves as capable of growing.

Of course, not every child who eats a limited diet is simply going through a phase. Some children have significant sensory sensitivities, medical conditions, or feeding disorders that require professional evaluation and support.

But for many families, replacing identity-based language with growth-oriented language can subtly change their child’s approach to mealtime, and to themselves. Children's identities are still under construction. The stories that they hear about themselves matter. When we describe eating as a journey rather than a personality trait, we leave the door open for children to discover that they are capable of more than they, or we, once believed.

item.title: Tickling the Tail of the AI Dragon
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Tickling the Tail of the AI Dragon

What OpenAI's incident teaches us about thresholds we can't see coming.

Posted July 22, 2026

Key points
  • OpenAI turned off model safety limits to test raw hacking ability.
  • The models found a hidden software flaw and broke into Hugging Face's systems.
  • The LLMs were hunting for the test's answers, not permission, and no one caught it live.
Source: Image by caro_oe92 from Pixabay

It was May 1946 in a room at Los Alamos. On the table sat a sphere of plutonium, about fourteen pounds, roughly the size of a softball. Around it, in two halves, was a shell of beryllium, a metal that bounces neutrons back where they came from. Louis Slotin was lowering the top half of that shell into place, a screwdriver wedged under the rim to keep the two halves from fully closing. He'd done this same motion many times. He and the team aptly called it tickling the dragon's tail.

The plutonium never moved. What moved was the shell around it, and the closer that shell closed, the more neutrons got reflected straight back into the plutonium core instead of escaping into the room. Somewhere in that narrowing gap lay a line, a point where the plutonium would start sustaining its own reaction instead of just fissioning here and there on its own. Nobody could calculate exactly where that line was. The only way to find it was to close the gap by hand and watch what happened.

On May 21st the screwdriver slipped. The shell closed the rest of the way. The room went blue, and Slotin, hands still on the assembly, had already absorbed enough radiation to kill him. He was dead nine days later.

The Light Comes Too Late to Help

That blue flash, the reaction often associated with this story, wasn't a warning. It was Cherenkov radiation. That's the glow you get when a burst of radiation moves through a medium like air or water. By the time Slotin saw it, the reaction had already gone critical and already delivered its dose. The light didn't give him a chance to stop anything. It told him what had already happened to his body. He knocked the shell apart a half second later because of his reflexes, not because the glow gave him time to think.

I think the blue flash is strangely relevant today. Because last week, Hugging Face disclosed that an AI agent had compromised its safety infrastructure, and OpenAI's account of their side of it reads like the same problem with a bit of its own blue light ending.

But let's take a step back. OpenAI had been testing two of their models with the usual safety constraints or refusals switched off. The task was specifically to see what the models could do without protective restrictions. This task was narrow and just a benchmark. But according to OpenAI, the models found a real vulnerability in the internal software and used it to exceed the evaluation itself. Eventually, the "unrestricted" LLM interacted with systems belonging to Hugging Face where it "hunted" for the answer key to the very test they'd been given.

That's the part that begins to align with Slotin—not the drama of what got touched, but the fact that there's no way to know the edge of a system except by approaching it. Slotin at least got a signal, however late. OpenAI got nothing built into the event itself—no flash, no glow, just their own security team noticing something odd in the logs. And Hugging Face separately noticed something odd in theirs. Two sets of humans, paying close attention, catching it after the fact. The reaction didn't announce itself. Someone had to go looking.

What the AI Dragon Doesn't Give You

I don't think this simply translates into a lesson for LLM development and safety. Slotin's danger was fixed in place, at least. The distance between those two beryllium halves was a known, physical thing, the same today as it would have been the day before. He wasn't just watching for the threshold, he was the one closing the gap that produced it. You can't really find where a system like that turns dangerous without pushing it there yourself. Whatever we're testing with these LLMs, I believe, works in a similar way.

Slotin's flash came too late to save him. Ours might not come at all. The warning, if there is one, isn't sitting in the reaction anymore, waiting to go off. It's sitting in whoever is still willing to watch and that includes OpenAI, Hugging Face and even you and me.
